subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on hydrocarbons, homologous series and polymers, then mark my answer against the Eduqas spec.
promptWeak: Explain crude oil, alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and polymers for GCSE Eduqas Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Crude oil is best described as:
options: A main source of hydrocarbons and a feedstock for the petrochemical industry
questions.explain: Crude oil is a mixture and a main source of hydrocarbons; it is a feedstock for the petrochemical industry.

questions.q: On what property does the separation of crude oil by fractional distillation depend?
options: Differences in boiling point of the fractions
questions.explain: Fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions with different boiling point ranges: smaller molecules with lower boiling points condense higher up the column.

questions.q: In a fractionating column, where do the fractions with the smallest molecules and lowest boiling points come out?
options: At the bottom, where it is hottest
They do not separate at all
At the top, where it is coolest
questions.explain: The column is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top. Small molecules have low boiling points and condense near the top; large molecules condense lower down.

questions.q: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
questions.explain: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH2n+2, for example methane CH4 and ethane C2H6.

questions.q: Which of these is a member of the alkane homologous series?
questions.explain: C4H10 (butane) fits CnH2n+2 (2x4+2 = 10). C2H4 and C3H6 are alkenes; C2H5OH is an alcohol.

questions.q: What is the purpose of cracking large hydrocarbon molecules?
options: To join small molecules into polymers
To make crude oil less flammable
To produce smaller, more useful molecules such as fuels and alkenes
questions.explain: Cracking breaks large, less useful hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful ones, including short-chain alkanes (fuels) and alkenes used to make polymers.

questions.q: When decane (C10H22) is cracked, one product is octane (C8H18). What is the other product?
questions.explain: Cracking must balance: C10H22 -> C8H18 + C2H4. The remaining atoms form ethene, an alkene, which fits CnH2n.

questions.q: Which statement about crude oil is correct?
options: It is a renewable resource that reforms quickly
It can be manufactured easily in a lab
It is a finite resource, and modern life is heavily dependent on hydrocarbons
questions.explain: Crude oil is a finite (non-renewable) resource that formed over millions of years, yet modern life depends crucially on hydrocarbons from it.

questions.q: Which functional group is present in all alcohols?
questions.explain: Alcohols all contain the -OH (hydroxyl) functional group, for example ethanol C2H5OH.

questions.q: Which functional group defines the carboxylic acids?
questions.explain: Carboxylic acids contain the -COOH (carboxyl) functional group, for example ethanoic acid CH3COOH.

questions.q: Members of the same homologous series share which feature?
options: The same functional group and similar chemical reactions
A different functional group in each member
questions.explain: A homologous series has the same functional group and general formula, so members show similar chemical reactions with a gradual trend in physical properties.

questions.q: What is the name of the second member of the carboxylic acids?
questions.explain: The first four carboxylic acids are methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid, so the second is ethanoic acid (CH3COOH).

questions.q: What is the molecular formula of propene, the second member of the alkenes?
questions.explain: Alkenes fit CnH2n. Propene has 3 carbons, so it is C3H6. C3H8 would be the alkane propane.

questions.q: Ethanol is oxidised. What type of organic product forms?
questions.explain: Oxidation of an alcohol produces a carboxylic acid; ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid.

questions.q: Which reaction is characteristic of alkenes because of their C=C double bond?
questions.explain: The C=C double bond lets alkenes undergo addition reactions, for example adding bromine across the double bond (which decolourises bromine water).

questions.q: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon in plenty of oxygen produces which products?
questions.explain: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water. Incomplete combustion (limited oxygen) can give carbon monoxide and soot.

questions.q: In addition polymerisation, what feature of the monomer allows it to form a polymer?
questions.explain: Addition polymerisation relies on the C=C double bond in an unsaturated monomer such as ethene, which opens to join many monomers into long chains.

questions.q: Ethene (CH2=CH2) polymerises to poly(ethene). What is the repeating unit?
questions.explain: In addition polymerisation the double bond opens, giving the saturated repeating unit -(CH2-CH2)- with no double bond and no small molecule lost.

questions.q: How does condensation polymerisation differ from addition polymerisation?
options: It uses monomers with a C=C double bond only
It produces no polymer at all
It joins monomers with two functional groups and loses a small molecule such as water
questions.explain: In condensation polymerisation each monomer has at least two functional groups; monomers join and a small molecule (often water) is released for each bond formed.

questions.q: DNA is a natural polymer. What are its monomer units called?
questions.explain: DNA is a polymer made from four different monomers called nucleotides. Other natural polymers include proteins (from amino acids) and starch/cellulose (from sugars).

specSource: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Chemistry specification (from 2016); Carbon compounds
